newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saddam is a foe nervous Gulf Arabs need - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Saddam is a foe nervous Gulf Arabs need - analysts.

text.p: The massive U.S. firepower being assembled in the Gulf may be reassuring for nervous Gulf Arab oil states but Iraqi President Saddam Hussein remains a foe they cannot afford to lose, analysts and diplomats said on Friday.
The Iraqi leader who invaded Kuwait in 1990 is flexing his muscles once again with a warning and a failed missile attack on American aircraft patrolling Iraqi airspace.

The U.S. responded by sending radar-evading stealth fighter-bombers and a second aircraft carrier to the Gulf, bringing B-52 bombers within striking range and a threat of "robust rules of engagement".
But Washington's Gulf Arab allies, despite harsh memories of Saddam's lightning invasion of Kuwait, fear weakening Iraq would play into the hands of the region's largest power, Iran.

"The Arabs since the (1979) Iranian revolution have relied on Iraq as a stabilising force in the face of Iranian desire for regional dominance and hegemony. Gulf states are happy to contain Saddam but they don't want him eliminated," said a Saudi analyst.
"It's a matter of a balance of power. Who dominates who. A divided and weak Iraq means weak Gulf states. Once a disease begins in one part of the body it spreads to the rest," he added.
Baghdad warned Kuwait on Thursday that permitting U.S. F-117A stealth aircraft to be based on its territory for possible strikes was "an act of war against the state of Iraq".
The fresh showdown between Washington and Baghdad has eased some of the pressure on Tehran which the United States accuses of sponsoring international terrorism. Iran denies the charges.
But the analysts and diplomats said Gulf Arab states, facing Iran across the Gulf, saw it as more of a threat than Iraq, traditionally a bulwark against non-Arab Iran.

"Iran remains much more of an overriding issue. Gulf states don't have a problem with the U.S. launching certain strikes against some targets. But they don't want to go much further. They can't threaten Saddam," said a Western diplomat.
Gulf Arab states backed Iraq's catastrophic war with Iran in the 1980s with billions of petrodollars. Since then Tehran has been a major security concern in the strategic region.
"Saddam Hussein believes he is the Arabs' eastern gate to prevent an Iranian threat that is on the rise as a result," said the Saudi analyst.

The six Gulf Arab states -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) -- have accused Iran of meddling in the affairs of other countries, a charge rejected by Tehran.
Gulf Arab fears heightened when troubled Bahrain in June accused Tehran of backing a Shi'ite Moslem plot to topple the government and install a pro-Iranian Islamic regime in Manama.

Analysts said the Gulf Arabs' wary response to the latest U.S. strikes action against Iraq -- only Kuwait offered a measure of support by expressing "full understanding" -- reflected fears of a further weakened Baghdad.

"The Americans have expanded the southern no-fly zone because Saddam moved troops into his own country in the north. Are they going to declare all of Iraq a no-fly, no-go zone?" asked a Gulf analyst. "What about Iran?"
The mood was reflected in a front-page editorial of the official UAE newspaper al-Ittihad on Friday.
It opened by saying: "The American strikes against Iraq will continue and will not stop as long as one Iraq soldier is present on Iraq's territory."

Even Saudi Arabia, key U.S. ally and launch pad for the 1991 Gulf War, distanced itself from last week's U.S. missile attacks on Iraq and said that if Washington had asked to use its bases for the operations it would have refused.
The Saudi analyst stressed that the Gulf states were locked in a vicious circle.
"The problem with Gulf Arab countries is they want somebody else to protect them. They can create well-trained armies but they keep relying on others. That's the dilemma," he said.
